'''''Annona squamosa''''' is a small, well-branched tree or [[shrub]] from the family [[Annonaceae]] that bears edible fruits called '''sugar apples''', '''sweetsops''' or '''custard apples'''.<ref name="aluka">{{Cite web|title=Compilation: Annona squamosa|url=https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/Annona.squamosa|work=Global Plants|publisher=JSTOR
|access-date=5 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="purdue">{{cite book|chapter=Sugar Apple: ''Annona squamosa''  | title =Fruits of Warm Climates| first = Julia |last = Morton  | author-link = Julia Morton | year = 1987| page = 69| publisher = Department of Horticulture & Landscape Architecture, [[Purdue University]]  |chapter-url = http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/sugar_apple.html | url-status= live <!--archive purposes only: | access-date = 17 April 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080405173228/http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/sugar_apple.html| archive-date= 5 April 2008-->}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]]; [[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=100 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref> It tolerates a tropical lowland climate better than its relatives ''[[Annona reticulata]]'' and ''[[Annona cherimola]]'',<ref name="aft">{{cite web
 |url=http://www.worldagroforestry.org/Sea/Products/AFDbases/AF/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=214
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110526114153/http://www.worldagroforestry.org/Sea/Products/AFDbases/AF/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=214
 |archive-date=26 May 2011
 |title=Current name: ''Annona squamosa'' 
 |access-date=17 April 2008 
 |website=AgroForestryTree Database 
 |publisher=International Center For Research In Agroforestry 
}}</ref> and is the most widely cultivated of these Annona species.<ref name=purdue/><ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN | access-date = 17 April 2008}}</ref>

''Annona squamosa'' is semi-(or late) [[deciduous]],<ref name="FNA">{{cite book
  | last =Kral | first =Robert
  |editor=Flora of North America Editorial Committee
  | chapter =''Annona squamosa'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 537. 1753 
  | title =Flora of North America North of Mexico
  | volume =3
  | chapter-url =http://beta.floranorthamerica.org/Annona_squamosa | access-date =5 September 2019}}</ref> and {{convert|3 to 8|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall,<ref name="aluka" /><ref name="FNA" /> similar to [[soursop]] (''[[Annona muricata]]'').<ref name="PIER">{{cite web
 | url = http://www.hear.org/pier/species/annona_squamosa.htm
 | title = Annona squamosa
 | access-date = 17 April 2008
 |website=[[Hawaiian Ecosystems at Risk project|Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]] (PIER) 
 | date = 5 January 2008
| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080512181628/http://www.hear.org/pier/species/annona_squamosa.htm| archive-date= 12 May 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> It is a native of [[tropical climate]] in the [[Americas]], and [[Spanish Empire|Spanish]] traders aboard the [[Manila galleons]] docking in the [[Spanish East Indies|Philippines]] brought it to Asia.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Noel  |last1=Amano |first2=Greg |last2=Bankoff |first3=David Max |last3=Findley  |first4=Grace |last4=Barretto-Tesoro |first5=Patrick|last5=Roberts |title=Archaeological and historical insights into the ecological impacts of pre-colonial and colonial introductions into the Philippine Archipelago |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0959683620941152 |date=Feb 2021 |journal=[[The Holocene]] |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=319-21 |doi=10.1177/0959683620941152|hdl=21.11116/0000-0006-CB04-1 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Custard Apple - Flora Sinensis 1656 (2950756).jpg|thumb|237px|[[Michał Boym]]'s drawing of, probably, the sugar-apple, in his ''[[Flora Sinensis]]'' (1655)]]

The [[atemoya]] or "pineapple sugar-apple", a hybrid between the sugar-apple and the [[cherimoya]], is common in Taiwan, although it was first developed in the [[United States]] in 1908. The fruit is similar in sweetness to the sugar-apple; as its name suggests, it tastes like pineapple.<ref name=purdue/>

==Description==
=== Fruits===
Fruits ripen 3 to 4 months after flowering.<ref name=purdue/><ref name="Grant2021">{{cite web |last1=Grant |first1=Amy |title=What Is Sugar Apple Fruit: Can You Grow Sugar Apples |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/trees/annona/sugar-apple-trees.htm |website=Gardening Know How |access-date=4 August 2023 |date=2021}}</ref> Aggregate and soft fruits form from the numerous and loosely united pistils of a flower which become enlarged and mature into fruits which are distinct from fruits of other species of the Annona genus.<ref name="aft" />

The round or heart-shaped, greenish yellow, ripened aggregate fruit is pendulous on a thickened stalk; {{convert|5 to 10|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} in diameter with many round protuberances and covered with a powdery bloom. Fruits are formed of loosely cohering or almost free carpels (the ripened pistels).<ref name="aluka" /><ref name=purdue/>

The pulp is white tinged yellow, edible and sweetly aromatic. Each carpel containing an oblong, shiny and smooth, dark brown to black, {{convert|1.3 to 1.6|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} long seed.<ref name=purdue/><ref name="aft" />
The fruit is spherical-conical, {{convert|5|-|10|cm|in|abbr=off|frac=4}} in diameter and {{convert|6|-|10|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, and weighing {{convert|100|-|240|g|oz|abbr=off}}, with a thick rind composed of knobby segments.<ref name=purdue/> The colour is typically pale green through blue-green, with a deep pink blush in certain varieties, and typically has a [[Epicuticular wax|bloom]]. It is unique among ''Annona'' fruits in being segmented; the segments tend to separate when ripe, exposing the interior pulp.<ref name=purdue/>

The flesh is fragrant and sweet, creamy white through light yellow, and resembles and tastes like [[custard]]. The seeds are coated with the flesh, It is found adhering to {{convert|13|to|16|mm|in|adj=mid|frac=8|-long}} seeds forming individual segments arranged in a single layer around a conical core. It is soft, slightly grainy, and slippery. The hard, shiny seeds may number 20–40 or more per fruit and have a brown to black coat, although varieties exist that are almost seedless.<ref name=purdue/><ref name=AFTDB>{{cite web|work=AgroForestryTree Database|title=''Annona squamosa''|url=http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/SEA/Products/AFDbases/AF/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=214|access-date=16 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070314161010/http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/SEA/Products/AFDbases/AF/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=214|archive-date=14 March 2007}}</ref> The seeds can be ground for use as an [[insecticide]], although this has not been approved by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] or EU authorities.<ref name=":0" /> The skin is shaped like a [[Reuleaux triangle]] coloured green and rough in texture.<ref name=purdue/> Due to the soft flesh and structure of the sugar apple, it is fragile to pressure when ripe.

The fruit has sweet whitish pulp, and is sold in tropical markets.<ref name="FNA"/> It is rarely cooked.<ref name=purdue/>

=== Flowers ===
Solitary or in short lateral clusters of 2–4 about {{convert|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long,<ref name="FNA" /> greenish-yellow flowers on a hairy, slender<ref name="aft" /> {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long stalk.<ref name="FNA" />  Three green outer petals, purplish at the base, oblong, {{convert|1.6 to 2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, and {{convert|0.6 to 0.75|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=16}}  wide, three inner petals reduced to minute scales or absent.<ref name="aluka" /><ref name="FNA" /> Very numerous stamens; crowded, white, less than {{convert|1.6|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} long; ovary light green. Styles white, crowded on the raised axis. Each pistil forms a separate tubercle (small rounded wartlike protuberance), mostly {{convert|1.3 to 1.9|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|0.6 to 1.3|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} wide which matures into the aggregate fruit.<ref name="aft" />

Flowering occurs in spring-early summer<ref name="FNA" /> and flowers are pollinated by [[nitidulidae|nitidulid]] beetles.<ref>McGregor, S.E. [http://gears.tucson.ars.ag.gov/book/ Insect Pollination Of Cultivated Crop Plants] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230326235745/http://gears.tucson.ars.ag.gov/book/ |date=26 March 2023 }} [[USDA]], 1976</ref> Its pollen is shed as permanent tetrads.<ref>Walker JW (1971) Pollen Morphology, Phytogeography, and Phylogeny of the Annonaceae.  Contributions from the Gray Herbarium of Harvard University, 202: 1-130.</ref>

=== Stems and leaves ===
Branches with light brown bark and visible leaf scars; inner bark light yellow and slightly bitter; twigs become brown with light brown dots (lenticels – small, oval, rounded spots upon the stem or branch of a plant, from which the underlying tissues may protrude or roots may issue).<ref name="aft" />

Thin, simple, alternate leaves occur singly, {{convert|5 to 17|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=off}} long and {{convert|2 to 6|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} wide, and are rounded at the base and pointed at the tip (oblong-lanceolate).<ref name="FNA" /> They are pale green on both surfaces and mostly hairless<ref name="aft" /> with slight hairs on the underside when young.<ref name="aluka" />  The sides sometimes are slightly unequal and the leaf edges are without teeth, inconspicuously hairy when young.<ref name="aft" /><ref name="PIER" />

The leaf stalks are {{convert|0.4 to 2.2|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, green, and sparsely pubescent.<ref name="aft" />

Sugar-apple is 73% water, 24% [[carbohydrate]]s, 2% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and contains negligible [[fat]] (table). In a reference amount of {{cvt|100|g}}, sugar-apple supplies 94 [[calorie]]s and is a rich source (20% or more of the [[Daily Value]]) of [[vitamin C]] and a moderate source of [[manganese in biology|manganese]] and [[Vitamin B6|vitamin B<sub>6</sub>]], with no other [[micronutrient]]s in significant content (table).

=== Chemistry ===
The [[diterpenoid]] [[alkaloid]] atisine (from the fruit's [[Tagalog language|Tagalog]] name {{wikt-lang|tl|atis}}) is the most abundant alkaloid in the root. Other constituents of ''Annona squamosa'' include the alkaloids oxophoebine,<ref name="pmid23678817">{{cite journal |author=Dholvitayakhun A, Trachoo N |display-authors=etal |year=2013 |title=Potential applications for ''Annona squamosa'' leaf extract in the treatment and prevention of foodborne bacterial disease |journal=Natural Product Communications |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=385–388 |doi=10.1177/1934578X1300800327 |pmid=23678817 |doi-access=free}}</ref> [[reticuline]],<ref name="pmid23678817" /> isocorydine,<ref name="pmid21342663">{{cite journal |author=Yadav DK, Singh N |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Anti-ulcer constituents of ''Annona squamosa'' twigs |journal=Fitoterapia |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=666–675 |doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2011.02.005 |pmid=21342663}}</ref> and methylcorydaldine,<ref name="pmid21342663" /> and the [[flavonoid]] [[quercetin-3-O-glucoside]].<ref name="pmid18997283">{{cite journal |author=Panda S, Kar A |year=2007 |title=Antidiabetic and antioxidative effects of ''Annona squamosa'' leaves are possibly mediated through quercetin-3-O-glucoside |journal=BioFactors |volume=31 |issue=3–4 |pages=201–210 |doi=10.1002/biof.5520310307 |pmid=18997283 |s2cid=38336427}}</ref>

[[Bayer AG]] has patented the extraction process and molecular identity of the annonaceous [[acetogenin]] [[annonin]], as well as its use as a [[biopesticide]], although this use has not been approved by [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|US]] or EU authorities.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Moeschler HF, Pfluger W |display-authors=etal |date=August 1987 |title=Insecticide US 4689232 A |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4689232 |access-date=3 December 2014}}</ref>  Other acetogenins have been isolated from the seeds,<ref name="pmid22609808">{{cite journal |author=Chen Y, Xu SS |display-authors=etal |year=2012 |title=Anti-tumor activity of ''Annona squamosa'' seeds extract containing annonaceous acetogenin compounds |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=142 |issue=2 |pages=462–466 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2012.05.019 |pmid=22609808}}</ref> and bark.<ref name="pmid2348205">{{cite journal |author=Li XH, Hui YH |display-authors=etal |year=1990 |title=Bullatacin, bullatacinone, and squamone, a new bioactive acetogenin, from the bark of ''Annona squamosa'' |journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=81–86 |doi=10.1021/np50067a010 |pmid=2348205}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Annona squamosa'' is native to the tropical Americas, but the exact origin is unknown.<ref name=purdue/> It is the most widely cultivated of all the species of ''Annona'', being grown for its fruit throughout the tropics and warmer [[subtropics]]  such as in India, Indonesia, Thailand, Taiwan, and China as far north as [[Suzhou, Jiangsu|Suzhou]] since its [[Columbian exchange|Old World introduction]] in the 16th century.<ref name=purdue/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inaturalist.ca/observations/37152727|publisher=iNaturalist|access-date=2 August 2026|title = Sweetsop (''Annona squamosa'')|date = January 2020}}</ref> It is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] as far north as Cuba, south [[Florida]], Mexico, Central America, and as far south as [[Bahia]], Brazil.<ref name=purdue/><ref name=aft/> It is an [[invasive species]] in some areas.<ref name=purdue/><ref name="aft"/><ref name="PIER"/>

==Climate and cultivation==
Like most species of ''Annona'', it requires a tropical or subtropical climate with summer temperatures from {{convert|25|°C|°F}} to {{convert|41|°C|°F}}, and mean winter temperatures above {{convert|15|°C|°F}}.<ref name=purdue/> It is sensitive to cold and frost, being defoliated below {{convert|10|C|F}} and killed by temperatures of a couple of degrees below freezing. It is only moderately [[drought-tolerant]], requiring at least {{Convert|700|mm}} of annual rainfall, and does not produce fruit well during droughts.<ref name=purdue/>

It will grow from sea level to an altitude of {{convert|2000|m|ft|abbr=off}} and thrives in hot dry climates, differing in its tolerance of lowland tropics from many of the other fruit bearers in the ''Annona'' family.<ref name=purdue/>

It is a prolific bearer, and it produces fruit within as little as two to three years. A five-year-old tree can produce as many as 50 sugar apples.<ref name=purdue/> Poor fruit production has been reported in Florida because there are few natural pollinators (honeybees have a difficult time penetrating the tightly closed female flowers); however, hand pollination with a natural fibre brush is effective in increasing yield. Natural pollinators include beetles ([[Beetle|Coleoptera]]) of the families [[Nitidulidae]], [[Staphylinidae]], [[Chrysomelidae]], [[Curculionidae]] and [[Scarabaeidae]].<ref name=purdue/><ref name=AFTDB/>

==Ecology==
It is a host plant for larvae of the butterfly ''[[Graphium agamemnon]]'' (tailed jay).{{scicn|date=August 2026}} In the [[Philippines]], the fruit is commonly eaten by the Philippine [[Lesser Short-nosed Fruit Bat|fruit bat]] (''kabag'' or ''kabog''), which spreads the seeds from island to island.{{scicn|date=August 2026}}

==Uses==
In [[traditional medicine| traditional Indian, Thai, and Native American medicines]], the leaves are boiled down with water, possibly mixed with other specific botanicals, and used in a [[decoction]] to treat [[dysentery]] and [[urinary tract infection]].<ref name=purdue/><ref name=" doi10.1016/j.hermed.2016.10.003">{{cite journal| author=Dholvitayakhun A, Trachoo N| title=Using scanning and transmission electron microscopy to investigate the antibacterial mechanism of action of the medicinal plant ''Annona squamosa'' Linn | journal=Journal of Herbal Medicine | year=  2016| volume=  7| pages= 31–36|doi =10.1016/j.hermed.2016.10.003|display-authors=etal| url=https://zenodo.org/record/884833 | doi-access=free}}</ref> In Indian medicine, the leaves are also crushed for use as a poultice, and applied to wounds.<ref name=" doi10.1016/j.hermed.2016.10.003" /> [[Extract]]s are used in ethnomedicine.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bisht |first1=Manohar S. |last2=Mahajan |first2=Shruti |last3=Chakraborty |first3=Abhisek |last4=Sharma |first4=Vineet K. |title=A high-quality genome assembly of ''Annona squamosa'' (custard apple) provides functional insights into an emerging fruit crop |journal=DNA Research |date=June 2025 |volume=32 |issue=3 |doi=10.1093/dnares/dsaf007|pmc=12116420 }}</ref>
In [[Haiti]], the fruit is known as ''cachiman'' and is used to simply make juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cachiman (''Annona reticulata'' L.) |url=http://caribfruits.cirad.fr/fruits_tropicaux/cachiman |website=Carib Fruits |access-date=8 November 2020}}</ref>
